title: How to make AI usage stick after training | Traq Collective
h1: How to make AI usage stick after training
metaDescription: AI training day rarely changes Monday. What makes usage stick is a visible win people can copy, a light bit of competition, and doing the first weeks together.
targetQuery: how to make AI usage stick after training
author: Nazir Dogan
dek: The session was never the hard part. The four weeks after it are.
intro: AI usage sticks when people see a real colleague winning with it, get a light reason to keep practising, and go through the first weeks together instead of alone. Training day changes nothing on its own. What changes daily behaviour is a visible example, a bit of friendly competition, and a shared push right after the session.
body: Most AI rollouts follow the same shape: a training session, a burst of use that week, then a slow drift back to old habits. Nobody is being lazy. A single event was never designed to change what people do every day, and without something to keep the habit alive it fades inside a month, same as any other training.

The first thing that works is making wins visible. Microsoft's own legal team ran a short internal series where staff shared their best AI use cases with each other, and Microsoft reports it saw close to a 50 percent rise in monthly active use of some Microsoft 365 apps afterward. You do not need a formal series to copy the idea: a Slack channel or a five-minute slot in the team meeting where one person shows the task AI just saved them time on gives everyone else a script to copy.

The second is a bit of friendly competition. When Microsoft's sales team ran quiz games and a scavenger hunt built around Copilot, daily active use jumped 31.7 percent, the clearest sign that people moved from occasional use to a real habit. A small business does not need a whole event: a weekly 'best prompt' shout-out or a lightweight team challenge does the same job at a fraction of the effort.

The third is doing it together rather than sending people off with a link. Microsoft's support organisation ran localised, peer-led sessions where colleagues walked each other through real workflows, and saw a measurable lift in daily use of the specific features they practised. For a small team, that just means blocking an hour where everyone opens the tool at the same time and works on their own real task with someone nearby to ask.
takeaway: Pick one tactic, not three: start a weekly 10-minute show-and-tell where someone shares the AI win that saved them the most time, and run it for the next month before adding anything else.

stat.claim: A light competition around a specific AI tool measurably shifted people from occasional to daily use, which is the habit that actually compounds.
